findings.location: suit-policy/policy-EN.tex:562-565 (Annotated TOC, Ch. 15 Sizing reference points)
findings.passage: Ch.~15  Sizing reference points ... Indicative orders of magnitude for a large research-intensive institution; FTE envelopes per layer; scaling levers and breakpoints.
findings.why: The annotated-TOC line anchors the Technical Reference sizing chapter on 'a large research-intensive institution' as the sole archetype, without tying it to the size-invariant minimal-necessary-set principle and without the explicit one-instantiation hedge used for the directly comparable archetype framing at line 632 (Ch.33, where 'research-intensive university' is qualified 'as one worked EU instantiation' and folded into the 'size- and jurisdiction-invariant' anchor). It is not routed through \loc{} or a category archetype, is not a labelled regulatory example, is not the sovereignty grid, and is not a sourced external statistic. While 'indicative orders of magnitude' hedges precision and 'scaling levers and breakpoints' gestures at scalability, the anchor archetype itself is asserted as the large research-intensive case, so an adopter from a smaller or teaching-focused family (LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB, UK teaching college) can read the sizing guidance as calibrated only for large research institutions. Survives as a genuine, borderline-but-non-refuted LOW finding.
findings.fix: Align with the size-invariant minimal-necessary-set principle, e.g. 'Indicative orders of magnitude anchored on a large research-intensive profile as one worked instantiation, with scaling levers and breakpoints down to the minimal functional set'; or add a half-clause noting the breakpoints scale down to small institutions. Mirror the Ch.33 'as one worked instantiation' hedge. No \loc{} needed since this paraphrases an external chapter title.

findings.passage: Four European regulatory instruments shape the cybersecurity and data-protection environment of universities ... The architecture of this report is designed to satisfy all four simultaneously.
findings.why: VERIFIED as surviving. The subsection lede generalises to "universities" tout court (line 509-510), and the crimson operational-consequence sentence (555-556) universalises the design claim. The localization registry DOES carry this regime through existing keys --- \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime}, \loc{data-protection-regime}, \loc{ai-regulation}, \loc{cross-border-transfer-regime} are defined in shared/localization-defaults.tex (lines 74-77) and bound per-archetype in every categories/*.tex (EU-PUB-RI, US-PUB-R1, US-PRIV-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB) --- yet this prose subsection hard-codes the EU GDPR/NIS2/AI-Act/Schrems-II quartet instead of routing through them. The title's word "European" gives only partial scoping; the body still binds non-EU editions to facts that do not apply to them. Note the candidate's claim that the registry "already routes the regime" is correct (the keys exist and are used in the companion); the defect is that THIS subsection bypasses them.
findings.fix: Scope the subsection title and lede as the EU-archetype instantiation (e.g. "For an adopter in the EU-PUB-RI family, four instruments shape...") or route through the existing \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime}/\loc{data-protection-regime}/\loc{ai-regulation}/\loc{cross-border-transfer-regime} keys with the EU quartet as a labelled example, mirroring the NIS2 item which already hedges with "Where the institution's jurisdiction has transposed..." (line 524).

findings.passage: Demonstrate through \textbf{concrete examples} that decentralised and segmented architectures are the norm at world-leading universities
findings.why: VERIFIED as surviving. Lines 740-749 state this as a report objective with no hedge or scoping. The reference-panel section (lines 2044-2069) carefully scopes its generalisation on "principles vs.\ implementations" and size-comparability (EPFL ~12,000 students, CERN governance-translatable), but this objective statement asserts a universal norm "at world-leading universities" and is not routed through the panel's selection criteria. The reference class implied (world-leading) misrepresents the suite's neutral-by-design adopter set (UK-RES teaching-led, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB).

findings.passage: Restrictive university digital policies simultaneously engage several fundamental rights protected by the \textbf{Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU} ... and the \textbf{European Convention on Human Rights}
findings.why: VERIFIED as surviving. The Charter/ECHR fundamental-rights block (4264-4320: EU Charter Arts.~13/11/10/7-8/1/31, ECtHR Sorguç/Yildirim/Bayatyan/Barbulescu, CJEU Scarlet) opens flatly stating that "Restrictive university digital policies simultaneously engage several fundamental rights protected by the Charter ... and the ECHR" --- presented as the generic legal basis for the adjustment right with no EU-scoping hedge and no \loc routing. The asymmetry is confirmed: the equal-treatment law IS routed through \loc{national-equal-treatment-law} (line 4189), the CRPD line hedges, the international-consensus paragraph (4322-4346) provides the jurisdiction-neutral anchor (UN HRC, UNESCO 195 countries, Magna Charta 94 countries) --- but the Charter/ECHR core is bound to "the institution" generically, misleading US/LATAM/AFR editions where neither instrument applies.
findings.fix: Frame the EU Charter / ECHR / CJEU / ECtHR body explicitly as the EU-archetype instantiation of the proportionality principle (with the CRPD/UN-resolution layer as the jurisdiction-neutral anchor), or introduce a \loc{fundamental-rights-instruments} key so non-EU editions substitute their constitutional/human-rights basis. Add one hedge sentence ("In EU-bound jurisdictions, these rights are grounded in...; elsewhere the equivalent national instruments apply").

findings.passage: the approach is validated by world-leading universities, international standards, and EU regulations

findings.passage: major cloud-based AI services (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, HuggingFace, AWS) is now part of the standard scientific working environment

findings.passage: a breach can affect the institution as a whole --- as recent breaches at major research universities have shown
findings.why: Verified verbatim at lines 147-149. findings.passage: These are not abstract philosophical references. They are \emph{binding law} in the EU and Council of Europe member states. An IT policy that systematically restricts digital access and monitors communications \emph{must} satisfy the proportionality requirements of these instruments.
findings.why: Verified in context. The sentence asserts the EU Charter / ECHR / CJEU-ECtHR regime as 'binding law' and states an IT policy 'must satisfy' its proportionality requirements as a standing obligation of the adopter. It is NOT routed through \loc{} (the body file contains zero \loc{} macros and the shared/localization-defaults.tex and categories/ directories do not yet exist), it is NOT hedged, and it is not a labelled comparative example. For the US-PUB-R1, US-PRIV-R1, LATAM-PUB and AFR-PUB archetypes these instruments are not binding, so the 'must satisfy' obligation is jurisdiction-specific presented as universal. NOTE: the candidate fix cites a \loc{regulatory-regime} 'default already reads ...' that does not actually exist in the repo; the key must be created, not assumed.
findings.fix: Generalise the binding claim once a regulatory-regime key exists: 'These are binding law in \loc{regulatory-regime}; where the adopter is so bound, an IT policy ... must satisfy the proportionality requirements; elsewhere they stand as a strongly persuasive proportionality benchmark.' Until the localization layer is created, hard-code the conditional softening (EU/CoE editions bound; other editions persuasive).

findings.passage: Article~13 of the EU Charter protects academic freedom as a \emph{fundamental right}. It applies to \emph{universities} --- that is not a stretch; it is the literal scope of the provision.
findings.why: Verified in context. Article 13 of the EU Charter is presented as the operative academic-freedom guarantee for the adopter ('it is the literal scope of the provision'), not labelled as one jurisdiction's exemplar. No \loc{} routing, no generic anchor. US/UK/LATAM/AFR archetypes protect academic freedom under different instruments, so this reads EU-as-universal.
findings.fix: Mark Article 13 as a labelled EU instance and add a generic anchor: 'In EU jurisdictions, Article 13 of the EU Charter protects academic freedom as a fundamental right; comparable jurisdictions protect it under their own constitutional or statutory instruments.'

findings.passage: \textbf{Lawful basis.} For a public university, the monitoring, audit and identity processing rests on Article~6(1)(e) --- processing necessary for a task carried out in the public interest ... and, where appropriate, Article~6(1)(f) legitimate interests (network and information security, expressly recognised in Recital~49) ...
findings.why: Verified in context. The opening 'For a public university' partially scopes institution-type, but the data-protection regime is assumed to be GDPR throughout and the analysis does not generalise to the private archetype (US-PRIV-R1, which cannot rely on 6(1)(e)) or to non-GDPR families (US-PUB-R1, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB). The institution-type conditional does not cure the regime assumption, and neither is parameterised in the file. The finding survives on the data-protection-regime axis.
findings.fix: State the GDPR Art.~6(1)(e)/(f) analysis as the EU-PUB-RI instantiation and add the generic shape: 'the controller identifies a lawful basis under its data-protection regime; a public-mission body typically relies on the public-interest task, a private body on legitimate interests / consent', so non-EU and private adopters are covered.

findings.passage: the \gls{gdpr}~\cite{gdpr} applies to every institution processing personal data, irrespective of size. The choice a small institution faces is therefore not ...
findings.why: Verified in context. The minimal-necessary-set / size-invariance argument is correctly do-not-flag, but the supporting no-threshold legal anchor is pinned to the GDPR and stated as binding 'every institution' with no jurisdictional qualifier. For US/LATAM/AFR families the GDPR is not the governing regime, so 'applies to every institution' is jurisdiction-specific even though the underlying no-size-threshold duty is generalisable. Not hedged, not \loc{}-routed.
findings.fix: Keep the size-invariance argument; generalise the legal anchor: 'a data-protection duty applies with no size threshold under the adopter's data-protection regime (the GDPR is the EU instance, applying irrespective of size)'.

findings.location: suit-policy/argumentation/argumentation-policy-body-EN.tex:35-37 (How to read this module, evidence methodology)

findings.passage: the central \gls{soc} owns the \gls{nis2} Article~23 reporting clock --- the 24-hour early warning, the 72-hour notification and the one-month final report
findings.why: Verified in context across Q8.1, Q8.5 and Q8.6. The answers assert NIS2 Art.~23 (clock), Art.~21(2)(d) (supply-chain), and GDPR Art.~15/16/17 (rights) and Art.~30 (RoPA) as the adopter's standing obligations ('the central SOC owns the NIS2 Article 23 reporting clock', 'NIS2 Article 21(2)(d) requires ongoing management'). findings.passage: creator of the first version of the suite (originally developed for the University of Luxembourg).
findings.why: VERIFIED in context. Line 248 hard-codes the concrete institution name "University of Luxembourg" directly in the canonical title-page prose. It sits OUTSIDE the trailing \loc{author-affiliation} call (which follows the closing period) and is NOT routed through any \loc{} key or category archetype. The localization registry confirms author-affiliation has an EMPTY generic default (shared/localization-defaults.tex:32), and the file header states that rendering with only the defaults "reproduces the present generic text UNCHANGED" — so this named institution renders identically in EVERY edition (EU-PUB-RI, US-PRIV-R1, AFR-PUB, etc.), embedding one concrete local fact into the suite's institution-neutral canonical text. None of the exemption grounds apply: it is not scoped via \loc{} or an archetype, not a labelled regulatory example, not the sovereignty concept/grid, not a sourced external statistic, and not hedged or conditional. It is precisely the kind of concrete local fact the localization layer exists to absorb. MODERATE (not HIGH) is correct: it is a provenance/origin statement, not a claim that binds or misleads adopters in another family.
findings.fix: Route the origin clause through a localization key: add \setloc{suite-origin-attribution}{} to shared/localization-defaults.tex (empty generic default) and reference it as ...creator of the first version of the suite\loc{suite-origin-attribution}. A Luxembourg edition then fills the key with "(originally developed for the University of Luxembourg)". Alternatively fold the origin fact into the existing \loc{author-affiliation} byline so the generic title page carries no hard-coded institution name.

findings.location: suit-solution/ch17-playbook-reading-EN.tex:110-118 (\S Vocabulary, Trajectory) and Table tab:pr-trajectory-detail line 217
findings.passage: \emph{greenfield}, \emph{brownfield Microsoft-centric}, \emph{brownfield hybrid} ... Each wave chapter develops the three principal trajectories (greenfield, brownfield Microsoft-centric, brownfield hybrid) in detail

The canonical trajectory taxonomy in the Vocabulary section names one of the five universal migration paths 'brownfield Microsoft-centric', and Table tab:pr-trajectory-detail (line 217) describes it as 'The most common starting point for institutions of the adopting institution's type' with the prose 'in front of the existing Microsoft estate; the Microsoft estate evolves at its own renewal pace'. The suite is demonstrably mid-refactor on exactly this label: a cross-chapter survey confirms ch22 already renamed it 'brownfield single-suite-centric' (line 125), ch24 'brownfield single-vendor' (line 123), ch26 'brownfield dominant-suite-centric' (line 136), while ch17/ch04/ch18/ch20/ch21/ch23/ch25/ch27 still carry the Microsoft-named form. This is a residual artefact, NOT a deliberate design constant, and is not the sovereignty grid/concept, not a sourced statistic, not routed through \loc{} or a category archetype.
findings.fix: Rename the trajectory throughout the taxonomy (ch17 Vocabulary item + Table tab:pr-trajectory-detail line 217) to the vendor-neutral form the suite already adopted elsewhere, e.g. 'brownfield single-suite-centric' / 'brownfield dominant-suite-centric'. Treat Microsoft only as a labelled example of a dominant suite. As the canonical definition point, fixing it here propagates to the residual uses in ch04, ch18, ch20, ch21, ch23, ch25, ch27.

findings.passage: Mostly 1--2, with Microsoft technologies dominant in identity, endpoint, and observability ... \textbf{Brownfield Microsoft-centric}, 7--10~year horizon. The most common European starting point; the playbook adds an open policy plane and an open observability collector layer in front of the existing Microsoft estate.
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic. The self-assessment trajectory matrix carries two compounded defects, confirmed verbatim: (1) it names Microsoft as the universal dominant brownfield vendor in the row label and prose, and (2) it asserts 'The most common European starting point' (line 327) -- an EU-only, unsourced frequency claim baked into a diagnostic instrument intended for every archetype (US/UK/LATAM/AFR). A reader in a non-EU, non-Microsoft family is handed a matrix row that does not describe them plus a Europe-specific market claim with no \cite. Not hedged, not an example, not routed through \loc{} or a category archetype, not a sourced statistic.
findings.fix: Rename the row to the vendor-neutral trajectory label (consistent with the ch17 fix) and replace 'The most common European starting point' with a jurisdiction-neutral phrase such as 'a common starting point for institutions whose estate is anchored on a single dominant productivity-suite vendor', dropping the EU-specific unsourced frequency assertion or routing any regional qualifier through a category archetype.

findings.location: suit-solution/ch06-identity-EN.tex:174-175 (\S 'Where it adds value'); ch12-observability-EN.tex:278-280 (\S 'Where it adds value')

Remove the 'majority of universities' / 'most European universities' quantifier, or attach a sourced external statistic if one exists; do not assert market share as background fact.

This is the most concrete vendor-lock instance of the trajectory-label defect -- it has moved past the label into product-named prose.
findings.fix: Replace 'Entra-based identity and Microsoft~365 estate' with the suite's neutral wording, e.g. 'the institution's incumbent proprietary identity suite and office-productivity estate', and 'Entra-to-OPA decision chain' with 'incumbent-IdP-to-policy-plane decision chain'. findings.location: suit-solution/ch06-identity-EN.tex:242-248 (Alternative 2, When it is the right choice)

findings.why: Confirmed: an unsourced empirical claim asserted as fact at lines 247-248, with a hard "ten or more years" figure and no citation. It is category-bound to the research-intensive family and is not a sourced external statistic (no \cite), not hedged (asserted after a colon as supporting fact), not a labelled example. Readers in other archetypes are given a magnitude they cannot rely on.
findings.fix: Either attach a source for the longevity claim or soften to a generic durability statement ("the pattern is a stable end-state, not merely a transition") without the specific cohort claim and the "ten or more years" figure.

findings.passage: It is also, for most universities at the time of writing, the most ambitious novelty in this architecture: very few institutions today operate a dedicated policy decision point separate from their applications and identity provider.
findings.why: Re-read in context (lines 41-46) the claim is NOT scoped via \loc{} or a category archetype, is not a labelled example, and is not a sourced statistic. The substantive empirical assertion -- 'very few institutions today operate a dedicated policy decision point separate from their applications and identity provider' -- is presented as a blanket fact about the entire adopter universe. The partial hedge 'at the time of writing' qualifies timing but not scope, and 'very few' is itself an unsourced universal generalisation. The phrase 'for most universities' also silently narrows the neutral adopter set (which includes non-university public/research bodies per the SUIT families) to universities. A US-PRIV-R1 or large EU-PUB-RI adopter that already runs an authorization platform is mis-described. Survives refutation: genuinely non-generic as written.
findings.fix: Soften to a scoped claim ('for many adopters, particularly those without a dedicated platform-engineering function, this is the most ambitious novelty...') or cite a sourced sector statistic. Replace 'most universities' with a neutral adopter role phrase (\loc{institution-type} / 'most adopters') so non-university families are not excluded.

findings.location: suit-solution/ch07-policy-EN.tex:359-360 (section: Common pitfalls / Over-centralisation of policy authoring)
findings.passage: The model mirrors the delegation pattern that successful federated IT governance has used over decades across higher-education and research institutions.
findings.why: Re-read in the 'Over-centralisation of policy authoring' pitfallbox (lines 352-361). The sentence asserts as universal historical fact that federated IT governance has been 'successful' and operated 'over decades' 'across higher-education and research institutions'. This is unsourced, uses an unhedged superlative ('successful ... over decades'), and presents one mature-IT-organisation archetype's experience as the universal norm; it is not routed through \loc{} or a category, not a labelled example, and not a sourced statistic. It does not generalise cleanly to younger or less-resourced adopter families (e.g. AFR-PUB, LATAM-PUB). Survives refutation.
findings.fix: Drop or soften the unsourced superlative and frame as a recommended pattern: e.g. 'mirrors the federated-governance delegation pattern common in mature higher-education and research IT organisations', removing the asserted 'successful ... over decades' historical universal.

findings.passage: D7.5 the policy plane is the most ambitious novelty for most universities
findings.why: Re-read at line 17: this is a build/decision-registry comment (not reader-facing prose) that mirrors the body claim and propagates the same 'universities' category narrowing of the otherwise neutral adopter set. Not routed through \loc{} or a category. Non-load-bearing because it is a comment, hence LOW, but it remains a maintained artifact that should track the softened body wording. Retained at LOW.
findings.fix: Align with the softened body wording; use 'adopters' rather than 'universities'. Cosmetic (comment), hence LOW.

findings.passage: It operationalises NIS2~Art.~21(2)(c) (business continuity and backup, through declarative redeployability) and (e) ... The layer contributes to 27001~A.8.32 (change management) and to NIST CSF \textsf{PROTECT} (PR.PS --- platform security).
findings.why: Confirmed in context. The Regulatory anchoring section states in the document's own voice, with no \loc{} routing and no example/conditional frame, that the compute layer 'operationalises NIS2 Art.21(2)' and that GDPR Art.32 obligations 'rest' on it. NIS2 is an EU directive binding only EU/transposing adopters; ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF are voluntary/US-origin frameworks an adopter may not have adopted. In a suite that is institution-, jurisdiction- and vendor-neutral by design, a reader in a LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB or US-PUB-R1 family is told their compute layer satisfies obligations under regimes that do not bind them. The cross-reference to \trchap{ch:regulatory-mapping} does not hedge or scope these operative sentences. This is not a sourced statistic, not a labelled regulatory example, and not the sovereignty concept/grid.
findings.fix: Frame the named instruments as a worked EU example or route them through the localization regime keys, e.g. open with 'Under \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime} (in the EU edition, NIS2 Art.21(2)...; ISO/IEC 27001 A.8.32; NIST CSF PR.PS as a cross-walk)...' and present the article-level mapping as illustrative rather than as a flat universal claim; route GDPR Art.32 via \loc{data-protection-regime}.

findings.passage: each institution's compute layer reflects its specific research mission and the context of its national research and education network.
findings.why: Confirmed in context. The closing clause of the precedents box asserts that every adopter has 'its national research and education network' (NREN) as context. This holds for EU-PUB-RI / UK-RES but is not universal: a private (US-PRIV-R1) or under-resourced (AFR-PUB) adopter may have no NREN relationship. The phrase is hard-coded in prose rather than routed through a localization key, so it universalises a fact that is not size/jurisdiction-invariant. Low severity because the surrounding box is clearly framed as precedent-not-template, which softens but does not remove the universalised NREN presumption.
findings.fix: Route the NREN reference through \loc{nren-name} (or soften to 'its national or regional research and education network, where one exists'), so an edition without an NREN can rebind or drop the phrase.

findings.passage: European research institutions participate in the EUDAT Collaborative Data Infrastructure (EUDAT CDI), whose B2 services suite ... operates across a network of more than twenty research and computing centres in over a dozen European nations.
findings.why: Verified in context (lines 138-155). The realworldbox is the storage layer's only set of 'precedents', and both exemplars (CERN EOS, EUDAT CDI) are EU/European research-computing references; EUDAT is explicitly bound to 'European nations'. The closing caveat (lines 149-154) only addresses scale transfer ('design lessons rather than direct templates' because relative teaching/admin/research proportions differ), not jurisdictional/family neutrality. For a non-EU adopter (US-PUB-R1, US-PRIV-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB) this presents EU-specific infrastructure as the universal precedent set, with no parallel exemplar from another family and no \loc{}/archetype parameterisation. Not refuted: not scoped to an archetype, not routed through \loc, and the hedge present does not cover the neutrality axis.
findings.fix: Either explicitly scope the box as a European-research-computing example (label it as one archetype's precedent), or add/parameterise a second non-EU exemplar (e.g. via a category archetype note) so adopters in US/UK/LATAM/AFR families see a representative precedent rather than EU infrastructure presented as universal.

findings.passage: The indicative staffing envelope set in the institution's adopted resourcing profile for a research-intensive institution spreads a small group of engineers across the OS-specific operations, with one engineer-equivalent dedicated to the unified posture schema
findings.why: Verified at lines 130-135: the staffing envelope is hard-wired to "the institution's adopted resourcing profile for a research-intensive institution". This phrase is NOT routed through \loc{} and is not a category archetype binding; it literally fixes the research-intensive archetype in prose. The localization registry is designed to parameterise exactly this (\loc{staffing-profile} / \loc{institution-type}) so the engineer-equivalent figure tracks the adopter's family (LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB, US-PRIV-R1, etc.). As written, a non-research-intensive adopter is handed a head-count that does not bind their context. Genuinely non-generic; survives refutation.
findings.fix: Route the profile through the localization key: replace "the institution's adopted resourcing profile for a research-intensive institution" with "\loc{staffing-profile}" (or "the resourcing profile of \loc{institution-type}"), so the engineer-equivalent figure scales with the adopter's archetype rather than assuming research-intensive.

findings.passage: Tight integration with the Microsoft estate that is already present at most European universities
findings.why: Verified in context: in Alternative 2 (Microsoft Sentinel), the "Where it adds value" paragraph asserts as universal fact that a Microsoft estate is "already present at most European universities." This is an unhedged, unsourced empirical prevalence claim that hard-codes the EU public/research family as the baseline. It is not routed through \loc{}, not a category archetype binding, not a labelled example, not a sourced external statistic, and not the sovereignty concept. The parallel Alternative 1 (Splunk) deliberately avoids any jurisdiction qualifier ("institutions with mature Splunk operations"), confirming this is an outlier. For US-PRIV-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB or AFR-PUB adopters the framing is neither established nor relevant.
findings.fix: Generalise the estate-prevalence claim, e.g. "Tight integration with a Microsoft estate where one is already present," dropping the "most European universities" universal assertion; or condition it on the archetype via the institution-type binding rather than asserting the EU family as the universal baseline.

findings.passage: It is the principal anchor of NIS2~Art.~21(2)(h) (cryptography policies and procedures) and contributes to the applicable data protection regime's encryption and pseudonymisation obligations (in the European Union, GDPR~Art.~32(1)(a)).
findings.why: Confirmed in context (lines 228-238). Within the same sentence and paragraph, the data-protection regime and the electronic-identification/trust-services regime are both routed through a generic 'the applicable ... regime' phrasing with EU instruments demoted to a parenthetical '(in the European Union, GDPR Art. 32(1)(a))' / '(in the European Union, eIDAS 2 ...)' example qualifier. NIS2 Art. 21(2)(h) alone is asserted flatly as 'the principal anchor' with no jurisdictional scoping. NIS2 is an EU directive; a non-EU adopter (US-PUB-R1, US-PRIV-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB) is bound by its own cybersecurity-baseline regime, not NIS2. As written it reads as a universal anchor, inconsistent with the surrounding GDPR/eIDAS2 treatment. Not the sovereignty concept, not a sourced external statistic, and not routed through a generic phrase or labelled as an EU example.
findings.fix: Route through a generic regime phrase and demote NIS2 to a labelled EU example, matching the GDPR/eIDAS2 treatment in the same sentence: e.g. 'the principal anchor of the applicable cybersecurity-baseline regime's cryptography requirements (in the European Union, NIS2 Art. 21(2)(h) --- cryptography policies and procedures)'.

findings.passage: An indicative envelope, for an R1 institution, would be on the order of two to four engineers shared with the platform-engineering function.
findings.why: Verified non-generic as written. "R1" is the US Carnegie research-classification label, not one of the six SUIT archetype families (EU-PUB-RI, US-PUB-R1, US-PRIV-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB), and it is not routed through any \loc{} key — confirmed by reading the exact passage (it uses the bare string "for an R1 institution", not \loc{institution-type} or \loc{staffing-profile}). Both keys exist in shared/localization-defaults.tex (line 21: institution-type = "a typical research-intensive institution"; line 23: staffing-profile), so a parameterised alternative is available and is the suite's intended idiom. The figure is framed as "An indicative envelope" (a baseline staffing number), not hedged as archetype-conditional or labelled as an example. The dominant neutral phrasing everywhere else in suit-solution (ch08, ch11, ch12, ch15, etc.) is "research-intensive institution"; only ch05 and this ch14 line carry the US-only "R1" label, confirming it as an inconsistent jurisdiction-anchored leak. A reader in an EU, UK, LATAM or African institution is given a universal-looking staffing figure pinned to a classification that does not exist in their jurisdiction. Not the sovereignty concept/grid, not a sourced external statistic, not a regulatory example, not the size-invariant minimal-necessary-set principle.
findings.fix: Replace "for an R1 institution" with the parameterised \loc{institution-type} (or \loc{staffing-profile}) phrasing, or scope it explicitly as an example for a research-intensive archetype (e.g. "for a research-intensive institution of the kind characterised in \loc{institution-type}, ..."), so the figure reads as archetype-conditional rather than universal.

findings.passage: Federation transactions per day (eduGAIN inbound and outbound combined): indicatively tens to hundreds of thousands.
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic. Line 80-82 names eduGAIN bare as the label of a generic *sizing dimension* ("Federation transactions per day"), not as part of the reference-instantiation stack label (where "Keycloak + SCIM + eduGAIN" is correct-by-design, as in ch01/ch03/ch06). As a per-layer sizing parameter it reads as if every adopter participates in eduGAIN, the European/eduGAIN-world interfederation. A US-PRIV-R1, LATAM-PUB, UK-RES or AFR-PUB institution federates through InCommon, a national hub, or no interfederation. The localization registry shared/localization-defaults.tex already defines \setloc{identity-federation-profile}{the academic identity interfederation} precisely to absorb this slot, yet the value is hard-coded in free prose here. Not scoped via \loc, not a category archetype, not a clearly-labelled regulatory example, not the sovereignty concept/grid, not a sourced external statistic (the figure is an explicitly indicative range, the name is the only fixed element).
findings.fix: Route the federation name through the existing registry key: replace "Federation transactions per day (eduGAIN inbound and outbound combined)" with "Federation transactions per day (\loc{identity-federation-profile} inbound and outbound combined)", so an institution edition / category archetype binds eduGAIN, InCommon, a national federation, or none. Mirror the same change in summary/solution-summary-EN.tex:436 which carries the same bare "eduGAIN" sizing reference.

findings.location: suit-solution/ch16-conformance-EN.tex:250-258 (\S Linkage with wave closure, Wave-to-test mapping)
findings.passage: Wave~1 (Identity) closes against the four Identity tests; Wave~2 (Observability) against the four Observability tests; ... Wave~6 (Endpoint) against the three Endpoint tests; ... Wave~9 (Lifecycle) against the three Orchestration tests.
findings.why: Verified against the table: the prose hard-codes per-layer test counts that exactly mirror row counts of Table~\ref{tab:cf-suite} (Identity/Observability/Network/Policy = 4 rows each -> "four ... tests"; Endpoint/Orchestration = 3 rows each -> "three ... tests"). The same chapter labels the table "illustrative" (lines 92, 98), instructs that tests "should be added or removed" (line 93), and states an institution "extends the illustrative reference suite ... to cover all four categories for each layer" (lines 213-215). Endpoint, Compute, Crypto and Orchestration are shown with only three categories, so an adopter reaching a Robust 3 must add rows, at which point these prose counts silently become wrong and drift from the authoritative per-wave \emph{exit criteria} headings in Chapters 18-27 (cross-referenced at lines 247-249). The counts are derived from an explicitly illustrative table, are not scoped by any \loc key or category archetype, and are not a sourced external statistic.
findings.fix: Replace the hard numeric counts with category/coverage language that does not encode a row total, e.g. "closes against the Identity-layer tests (all four categories)" / "against the Endpoint-layer tests across the categories it implements", and state once that the authoritative per-wave subset is the \emph{exit criteria} heading of the corresponding wave chapter. Avoid restating counts derived from the illustrative table.

findings.location: suit-solution/ch16-conformance-EN.tex:184-185 (\S How to run a conformance day, Cadence paragraph)
findings.passage: The full suite is exercised at minimum once per year.
findings.why: Confirmed: the cadence is stated at the point of declaration as an unqualified universal floor ("at minimum once per year") covering "the full suite". The down-scaled / managed-service carve-out exists only later, in the reporting section (lines 227-233), and is not attached to this cadence sentence. A down-scaled or teaching-led adopter that consumes most layers as managed or mutualised services answers replaceability via provider exit terms rather than self-run tests (acknowledged at lines 230-233), so a fixed annual floor for the full suite over-reaches the neutral family set. The value is not a sourced statistic and is not scoped via \loc.
findings.fix: Soften to a recommended default scoped to self-operated layers, e.g. "For layers the institution operates itself, the full applicable suite is exercised at a regular cadence (a yearly minimum is a reasonable default for a research-intensive operator); a down-scaled adopter sets the cadence in proportion to the layers it self-operates."

findings.location: suit-solution/ch16-conformance-EN.tex:272-274 (\S Linkage with wave closure, closing paragraph)
findings.passage: becomes an artefact that the institution can share with peers in the international network anticipated by this Reference.
findings.why: Confirmed in context: the closing sentence presumes "the international network anticipated by this Reference" as a given framing. While "can share" hedges the action as optional, the definite-article reference to a single anticipated international peer network bakes in a non-neutral, EU-research-network-flavoured assumption that does not hold uniformly for LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB or US-PRIV-R1 adopters. It is not routed through any \loc/network key or category archetype and is not a sourced statistic; it is mildly aspirational rather than misleading, hence LOW.
findings.fix: Soften to an optional, archetype-neutral benefit, e.g. "and, where the institution participates in a peer or research-network community, an artefact it can share with peers"; or route the network framing through an existing \loc{peer-network} key so it matches the active category archetype.

findings.passage: The most common starting point for institutions of the adopting institution's type.
findings.why: The trajectory label "Brownfield Microsoft-centric" is a defined category archetype (see lines 110-118) and is correct by design, so the vendor name in the row label is NOT the defect. The surviving defect is twofold: (1) "the most common starting point" is an unhedged universality claim asserted across every archetype family, whereas Microsoft-estate dominance is true only for some cohorts (EU/US research universities) and not for others (LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB, Google Workspace shops); and (2) "institutions of the adopting institution's type" is a literal in-prose stand-in for the \loc{institution-type} key (which exists in shared/localization-defaults.tex line 21, defaulting to "a typical research-intensive institution"). The hard-coded phrase will not track an edition override, and ch17 uses no \loc{} expansions at all.
findings.fix: Hedge the frequency claim (e.g. "A common starting point, especially for institutions with a large Microsoft 365 / Entra estate") and route the cohort reference through \loc{institution-type} instead of the literal "institutions of the adopting institution's type", so the phrasing tracks the localization registry.

findings.passage: Frequent among research-intensive institutions of the adopting institution's type.
findings.why: "institutions of the adopting institution's type" is a literal in-prose paraphrase of the \loc{institution-type} key, which is defined in shared/localization-defaults.tex:21 as "a typical research-intensive institution". Hard-coding the cohort descriptor in prose means it will not track an edition's override of institution-type and duplicates a fact the localization registry already owns. The same literal phrase recurs at ch18-wave0-foundations-EN.tex:132, confirming it is an un-routed manual stand-in rather than a \loc{} expansion. It is also internally redundant: "research-intensive ... institution-type" restates the key's own default of "a typical research-intensive institution".
findings.fix: Replace the literal "institutions of the adopting institution's type" with the \loc{institution-type} expansion (or a key derived from it) so the cohort phrasing is owned by shared/localization-defaults.tex and tracks any edition override, and drop the redundant "research-intensive" qualifier already implied by the key's default.

findings.passage: the management-body-accountability obligation of the applicable national NIS2 transposition ... and of \gls{gdpr}~Art.~24 (controller responsibility)
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic. The target file contains zero \loc{} usage. In the Regulatory-anchoring section, NIS2 is correctly wrapped as 'the applicable national NIS2 transposition' (the NIS2 article number trailing as a labelled 'corresponding to' example), but GDPR Art. 24 (controller responsibility) is named directly as a co-equal governance anchor with NO \loc{} routing and NO baseline/equivalent hedge. The suite's own localization-defaults.tex already defines the keys data-protection-regime ('the institution's applicable data-protection regime') and cybersecurity-baseline-regime, and localization-guide-EN.tex:237 explicitly prescribes framing anchors as 'the institution's applicable data-protection... regime, giving GDPR/NIS2/eIDAS as the worked instantiation'. The companion shared/regulatory-applicability-EN.tex:79 already follows this convention ('GDPR Art. 32 in the baseline; an equivalent exists in every...'). For the US-PRIV-R1, US-PUB-R1, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB families there is no GDPR controller-responsibility duty. The bare GDPR Art. 24 naming is therefore an internally inconsistent EU overreach, not a labelled example and not hedged.
findings.fix: Route the data-protection anchor through \loc{data-protection-regime} and demote the GDPR article to a labelled instantiation, mirroring the existing convention: e.g. '...and of the controller-responsibility duty of \loc{data-protection-regime} (GDPR Art. 24 in the EU baseline; an equivalent exists in most regimes), when read at institutional level.' Defer full per-regime detail to \trchap{ch:regulatory-mapping}. The EU/CoE default in localization-defaults.tex keeps the EU edition rendering unchanged.

findings.passage: For the most common brownfield position --- an institution whose identity layer already runs on the cloud identity service of a dominant office-productivity suite vendor --- Wave~1 is the wave in which the institution's relationship with that incumbent proprietary identity suite is restructured rather than replaced.
findings.why: The brownfield section title is already genericised to "incumbent proprietary identity suite" (no vendor named), but the body frames a single archetype --- an institution on "the cloud identity service of a dominant office-productivity suite vendor" with "proprietary conditional-access expressions" and an "office-productivity estate" --- as "the most common brownfield position" for every adopter. The defining vendor-estate role is asserted in prose rather than routed through a \loc{} key or category archetype, so a US-PRIV-R1, LATAM-PUB or AFR-PUB adopter on a different incumbent (e.g. an in-house LDAP or another federation stack) reads the office-productivity-suite case as the default brownfield path. NOTE: the original candidate over-attributed this to Entra/Microsoft 365 by name; the file never names a vendor --- the surviving defect is the unhedged "most common" + single-archetype framing and the un-parameterised vendor/estate role, not a literal vendor name.
findings.fix: Soften "the most common brownfield position" to "a common brownfield position"; route the vendor/estate role through a \loc{} key (e.g. \loc{incumbent-identity-suite-vendor}) and a category archetype so editions on other incumbents read correctly; present the office-productivity-suite + conditional-access specifics as one illustrative archetype rather than the assumed estate for all adopters.

findings.passage: An institutionally agreed proportion of applications --- a common expectation is at least eighty percent in a brownfield trajectory --- has been migrated, with the remainder either in a documented schedule or in the documented exception register.
findings.why: A hard, unsourced magic number (eighty percent) is embedded in prose as a migration-coverage threshold and presented as a generic "common expectation". It is not a sourced external statistic, not a named design constant (unlike the 5-dimension grid / 9 layers patterns), and not routed through a \loc{} key. The same sentence already defers the real figure to "an institutionally agreed proportion", which makes the hard-coded 80% both redundant and a drift hazard --- institutions of differing size and maturity will set it differently, yet the prose asserts a universal figure.
findings.fix: Drop the hard figure, or move it to a single per-edition \loc{} key / named design constant (e.g. \loc{migration-coverage-target}) set once per institution edition, rather than asserting "at least eighty percent" as a universal expectation in the prose.

findings.passage: Specific architectures discussed in the fora of the national research and education network and its associated security incident response team, and in the security operations environments of large research infrastructures...
findings.why: Confirmed non-generic as written. The chapter contains no \loc{} call at all, yet the localization registry already provides the exact canonical role phrases this prose duplicates verbatim: shared/localization-defaults.tex:57 sets nren-name to "the national research and education network" and line 58 sets nren-csirt to "the NREN CSIRT". The category archetypes rebind these to materially different structures (UK-RES->Janet, US-PRIV-R1->Internet2 via regional R&E network, LATAM-PUB->RedCLARA-member NREN, AFR-PUB->network-operator CSIRT). By spelling the Layer-0 default inline the chapter bypasses the parameterisation system, so an institution whose family has no single NREN or a differently-structured CSIRT cannot rebind this through its edition. The realworldbox label does not save it: the defect is the hard-coded role phrase, not the precedent example.
findings.fix: Route the two facts through the registry: replace the spelled-out phrase with \loc{nren-name} and \loc{nren-csirt} (e.g. "the fora of \loc{nren-name} and \loc{nren-csirt}"). Keep the cautious "would benefit from being consulted" framing unchanged.

findings.passage: with sufficient address space for the planned research and BYOD growth
findings.why: Verified non-generic as written. The phrase appears once in the chapter, is not routed through \loc{}, is not hedged with 'as applicable' or 'e.g.', and is not bound to a category archetype. In a Pre-requisites section meant to apply to every adopter, it hard-codes 'research and BYOD growth' as THE address-space sizing drivers, presenting a research-intensive / BYOD profile as the universal planning assumption. A teaching-focused, AFR-PUB or LATAM-PUB adopter may have neither significant research growth nor a BYOD program as its dominant driver. Refutation criteria do not apply: no \loc{} scoping, no archetype binding, not a labelled example, not a sourced statistic, not the sovereignty grid/minimal-necessary-set, and not already hedged.
findings.fix: Soften to growth drivers in general, e.g. 'with sufficient address space for the institution's planned growth (research, BYOD, IoT, or other drivers as applicable)', so the example drivers read as illustrative rather than mandatory.

findings.passage: authorisation logic resides primarily in the incumbent identity-suite vendor's conditional-access expressions and in that vendor's application-level configuration
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic. shared/localization-defaults.tex:104 registers \setloc{incumbent-identity-suite-vendor}{a pure-commercial identity provider}, and instantiations/lu-university-of-luxembourg/set.tex:113 rebinds it to 'Microsoft Entra ID with Conditional Access' — proving the incumbent-vendor role is designed to be parameterised per edition. Yet ch22 hard-codes the role phrase 'the incumbent identity-suite vendor' in prose and consumes \loc{} nowhere in the file. An edition that rebinds the vendor role leaves this brownfield-MS section inconsistent with the rest of the suite. Not scoped, not an example, not the sovereignty concept, not a sourced statistic.
findings.fix: Replace the hard-coded role phrase with \loc{incumbent-identity-suite-vendor} (adjusting possessive grammar) so this section tracks any edition's vendor binding like the rest of the suite.

findings.passage: A standalone policy decision point is deployed alongside the incumbent identity suite. For each conditional-access expression identified in Wave~1's inventory, an equivalent policy is authored ... The vendor's conditional-access expression remains authoritative
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic. 'conditional-access expressions' / 'the incumbent identity suite' / 'the vendor's conditional-access expression' name a vendor-specific authorisation construct — the LU instantiation confirms 'Conditional Access' is the Microsoft Entra mechanism the key resolves to. The mechanism term and vendor reference are presented as the generic brownfield-MS pattern, neither routed through \loc{incumbent-identity-suite-vendor} nor labelled as an exemplar; an institution whose incumbent suite uses a differently-named mechanism is described inaccurately. Same defect class as GEN-w4-vendor-loc in the adjacent paragraph.
findings.fix: Route the vendor reference through \loc{incumbent-identity-suite-vendor} and generalise the mechanism term, e.g. 'the incumbent suite's conditional-access (or equivalent) expressions', keeping conditional-access as a labelled exemplar.

findings.passage: third-country data egress under \gls{gdpr}~Art.~32 and the \emph{Schrems~II} framework
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic as written. Line 124 presents Schrems II (CJEU C-311/18) + GDPR Art.32 as THE frame for any adopter's third-country egress, inside a chapter (lines 107-113) that states institutions of all archetypes choose this scenario. The suite's own established convention scopes this differently: companion-body-EN.tex:415 says 'in the worked EU instantiation, the \emph{Schrems~II} cumulative regime applies', and ch10-storage-EN.tex:281 routes the same fact through \loc{cross-border-transfer-regime}. The key \setloc{cross-border-transfer-regime} exists in shared/localization-defaults.tex:78 and is consumed by a sibling solution chapter, so the localization mechanism is available and the bare EU-doctrine assertion here is an anomaly, not the design pattern.
findings.fix: Route the regime through \loc{cross-border-transfer-regime} (and \loc{data-protection-regime}) and demote Schrems II to a labelled EU example, e.g. 'third-country data egress under the adopter's \loc{cross-border-transfer-regime} (in the EU, GDPR Art.~32 read with the \emph{Schrems~II} doctrine)', matching the companion-body and ch10 framing.

findings.passage: A pilot that demonstrates a documented egress policy under \emph{Schrems~II} conditions produces an artefact that the institution can show to its governance body, its data protection officer, and the regulators
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic. Lines 142-145 bind 'under Schrems II conditions' to every adopter of the scenario and assume a GDPR-style 'data protection officer' role universally, with no \loc{} routing and no 'in the EU' hedge. A non-EU archetype (US-PRIV-R1, AFR-PUB, LATAM-PUB) is not governed by Schrems II and may have a different or absent DPO construct. The minimal-necessary-set / sovereignty grid is generic, but this regulatory anchor and role phrase are not, and the suite elsewhere scopes both (companion-body-EN.tex:415; data-protection function routed via localization).
findings.fix: Generalise the transfer condition via \loc{cross-border-transfer-regime} and the data-protection-function role phrase, keeping 'Schrems II conditions' only as a parenthetical EU example.

findings.passage: The Researcher-LLM-API scenario is the principal locus where the EU AI Act applies: Art.~2(6) ... with Art.~50 ... still applicable
findings.why: VERIFIED non-generic. Line 275 asserts 'the EU AI Act applies' as the scenario's AI-governance frame with no scope to EU adopters. A suite-wide grep shows this is the ONLY bare 'AI Act applies' assertion in the solution; the established convention is conditional/exemplary (companion-body-EN.tex:419 'where one exists --- e.g. Art.~2(6) of the EU AI Act'; regulatory-applicability lists the AI Act as one instrument). The key \setloc{ai-regulation}{the adopter's applicable AI-governance regime} exists in shared/localization-defaults.tex:77 precisely so non-EU families are not told the EU AI Act binds them. NOTE: the GDPR Art.~25/35/32 and NIS2 Art.~21(2)(a) references in the same paragraph are cross-referenced to \trchap{ch:regulatory-mapping} (lines 284-286), consistent with the deliberate regulatory-mapping pattern, so the surviving defect is specifically the unconditional 'AI Act applies' assertion.
findings.fix: Frame the AI-governance anchor via \loc{ai-regulation} and present the EU AI Act articles as the EU instantiation, e.g. '...is the principal locus where the adopter's \loc{ai-regulation} bites; in the EU, the AI Act Art.~2(6) (research exemption) is typically invoked, with Art.~50 still applicable...', matching the companion-body 'where one exists' phrasing.

findings.passage: Patterns reported in the national research and education network's community fora and at sector conferences include mixed-OS estates
findings.why: Confirmed in context. The literal phrase "the national research and education network" is verbatim the Layer-0 generic role phrase bound to the localization key nren-name (shared/localization-defaults.tex:57: \setloc{nren-name}{the national research and education network}). The \loc{nren-name} convention is actively used in suite prose (e.g. suit-policy/companion/companion-body-EN.tex:374-440), so hard-coding the phrase here bypasses localization: an institution edition that overrides nren-name (RESTENA, Internet2, Janet, RENATER, SURF, RNP, SANReN-TENET, etc.) cannot localize this sentence, and the prose silently diverges from every other NREN reference. This is NOT a sourced external statistic (the realworldbox itself states "Public documentation ... is uneven" and reports patterns, not a cited figure), NOT the sovereignty concept/grid, NOT a labelled regulatory example, and NOT already routed through \loc{}. Survives adversarial refutation.
findings.fix: Route the reference through the existing key: replace the literal phrase with \loc{nren-name}'s ("... reported in \loc{nren-name}'s community fora and at sector conferences ..."). The generic default text stays identical while editions can substitute the concrete NREN. (Note: the same literal phrase also occurs in ch31-institutional-precedents-EN.tex:199,220 and could be normalised in a follow-up, but those are out of scope for this file.)

findings.passage: It is the principal anchor of the applicable national cybersecurity baseline regime (the national NIS2 transposition, NIS2~Art.~23: incident reporting --- 24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification, one-month final report)
findings.why: Confirmed genuine. The localization key \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime} exists with a jurisdiction-neutral default ('the applicable supranational and national legal framework', localization-defaults.tex:74) and the EU-PUB-RI archetype already binds it to the NIS2 text (categories/eu-pub-ri.tex:105). The wave-chapter prose nonetheless hard-codes 'the national NIS2 transposition' plus the precise EU-only 24h/72h/one-month timeline directly in running text, not routed through \loc and not labelled as an EU example. The same paragraph uses \loc{national-dpa} (line 279), proving the author knows the mechanism but bypassed it for the NIS2 content. A US-PUB-R1/US-PRIV-R1/LATAM-PUB/AFR-PUB/UK-RES edition is bound by no NIS2 obligation, so a non-EU reader is told their wave anchors a regime they do not have. Not the sovereignty grid, not an external statistic, not a labelled example, not hedged.
findings.fix: Route the regime through \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime} / \loc{nis2-national-transposition}, and present the Art.~23 article + 24h/72h/one-month timeline as a clearly-labelled EU example (e.g. 'in EU jurisdictions, e.g. NIS2~Art.~23 ...') or push the EU-specific article/timeline mapping into the EU-PUB-RI archetype so non-EU editions render their own baseline.

findings.passage: The wave also operationalises the same regime's incident-handling and effectiveness-assessment duties (NIS2~Art.~21(2)(b) and Art.~21(2)(f), the latter through audit-replay exercises).
findings.why: Confirmed genuine, same EU-only dependency as GEN-w7nis2univ. Art.~21(2)(b)/(f) are EU directive provisions stated as duties 'the wave operationalises' in running prose, with no EU scoping, no \loc routing, and no example label, while neutral \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime} and an EU archetype binding both exist. Non-EU families have no NIS2 Art.~21.
findings.fix: Make conditional on the EU-PUB-RI archetype or wrap as a labelled EU example alongside \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime}, consistent with the GEN-w7nis2univ fix.

findings.passage: It operationalises NIS2~Art.~21(2)(c) (business continuity through declarative redeployability) and (e) (security in development and maintenance, through SLSA-level supply-chain attestations).
findings.why: Confirmed in context. The immediately preceding sentence (lines 265-269) correctly routes the obligation through the generic 'applicable data-protection regime's security-of-processing obligation' with GDPR Art. 32 / Art. 5(1)(c) as labelled 'e.g.' examples. The NIS2 sentence breaks that pattern: it asserts 'It operationalises NIS2 Art. 21(2)(c)... and (e)' as an unconditional property of the wave, with no generic-regime wrapper and no 'e.g.' scoping. NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) is an EU-only instrument; a US-PUB-R1 / US-PRIV-R1 / UK-RES / LATAM-PUB / AFR-PUB adopter is bound by no NIS2 article. The asymmetry with the adjacent GDPR treatment makes this a genuine, non-hedged locality-as-universal assertion (not a labelled example, not the sovereignty grid, not an external statistic, not \loc-routed).
findings.fix: Mirror the preceding GDPR sentence pattern: wrap in the generic cybersecurity-baseline regime with NIS2 as a labelled EU example, e.g. 'It contributes to the applicable cybersecurity-baseline regime's business-continuity and secure-development obligations (e.g. NIS2 Art. 21(2)(c) and (e), through declarative redeployability and SLSA-level supply-chain attestations).' If the registry exposes a key such as \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime}, route through it.

findings.passage: The wave is the principal anchor of 27001~A.8.32 (change management) at scale and contributes to NIST CSF \textsf{PROTECT} (PR.PS) and \textsf{RECOVER} (RC.RP).
findings.why: Confirmed in context. ISO/IEC 27001 A.8.32 and NIST CSF function/category codes are voluntary, elective frameworks whose adoption varies by archetype (NIST CSF is predominantly a US-family reference; ISO 27001 certification is opt-in). The clause states them as unconditional properties of the wave ('is the principal anchor of 27001 A.8.32 at scale'), while the GDPR clause in the same section is scoped with 'e.g.'. This is a real, un-hedged framework-adoption assumption rather than a labelled example or the sovereignty concept. Severity LOW because these are voluntary standards (not jurisdiction-binding regulation) and detailed cross-references already live in \trchap{ch:regulatory-mapping}.
findings.fix: Make adoption conditional, e.g. 'Where the institution adopts ISO/IEC 27001 it is the principal anchor of A.8.32 (change management) at scale; for NIST CSF adopters it contributes to PROTECT (PR.PS) and RECOVER (RC.RP).' Keep the per-wave prose framework-neutral and let \trchap{ch:regulatory-mapping} carry the detail.

findings.passage: Under the EU AI Act, Art.~53 (obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, including model documentation and provenance) is the locus where the wave's lifecycle discipline applies to AI artefacts.
findings.why: Verified in context. The EU AI Act is an EU-only instrument stated as THE universal locus ('is the locus') for AI-artefact lifecycle discipline, with no scoping for non-EU adopters (US-PUB-R1, US-PRIV-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB). Unlike the immediately preceding NIS2 clause, which is routed through 'applicable national ... transposition' wording, the AI Act clause carries no 'applicable' hedge, no '\loc{}' routing, and no 'in the EU' label. The suite already provides a \loc{ai-regulation} key ('the adopter's applicable AI-governance regime') precisely for this. A non-EU reader is told an inapplicable statute governs their lifecycle stage.
findings.fix: Route the AI-governance anchor through \loc{ai-regulation} and present the EU AI Act Art.~53 as a labelled EU example, e.g. 'Under \loc{ai-regulation} (in the EU, Art.~53 of the AI Act for general-purpose AI model providers ...)'.

findings.location: suit-solution/ch28-cross-cutting-EN.tex:116-117 (\S Training and skills development, "Research-network and peer-institution mutualisation")
findings.passage: with peer institutions through its pan-European or regional research-network federation
findings.why: "pan-European" names an EU-specific federation family (GEANT-style) and presents it as the primary default mutualisation channel for every adopter ("pan-European or regional"), not as a scoped EU example. A US-PUB-R1, US-PRIV-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB or AFR-PUB institution has no pan-European federation. The surrounding prose already uses the generic role phrase "its national research and education network", and the localization registry (shared/localization-defaults.tex) provides verified jurisdiction-neutral keys (peer-nren-roster = "peer NRENs in comparable jurisdictions...", research-backbone-scale = "the regional research backbone...", nren-name), so the hard-coded continental geography is a non-generic outlier not routed through \loc{}.
findings.fix: Route the federation context through localization instead of hard-coding a continent. Replace "through its pan-European or regional research-network federation" with "through \loc{peer-nren-roster}" (or add a dedicated key, e.g. \loc{research-network-federation} defaulting to "its regional research-and-education-network federation"), letting an EU edition fill in the pan-European/GEANT specifics. Minimal alternative: drop "pan-European or" and keep the neutral "regional research-network federation".

findings.passage: Pattern: eduroam <-> TAC-aware Wi-Fi ... The pattern in which the institution's eduroam participation continues for inter-institutional roaming while a TAC-aware RADIUS attachment governs intra-institutional connections.
findings.why: Confirmed in context. The chapter explicitly states (lines 17-20) that patterns are described 'at the level of operational principle rather than at the level of specific tooling'. The five sibling patterns honour this: every commercial product and incumbent service is abstracted to a generic role phrase ('incumbent enterprise directory', 'per-volume-priced commercial SIEM', 'incumbent commercial hypervisor', 'enterprise storage array', 'open-source distributed storage'). eduroam is the lone hard-coded named external service, and 'the institution's eduroam participation continues' presumes every adopter participates in eduroam / has an NREN identity interfederation. True for EU-PUB-RI / UK-RES, an assumption for some private or non-NREN adopters in other archetype families. It is not a sourced statistic, not a labelled example, not the sovereignty grid, and not routed through \loc.
findings.fix: Route the roaming service through an NREN-service \loc key (reuse \loc{nren-service-catalogue}'s federated-Wi-Fi role or add a 'federated-roaming-service' key whose generic default is 'the research/education-network federated roaming service (e.g. eduroam)'). Keep 'eduroam' only as a parenthetical labelled example, and soften 'the institution's eduroam participation' to 'the institution's federated-roaming participation, where it participates'.

findings.passage: The eduroam technical profile is treated as inviolate: extending it with institution-specific attributes for inter-institutional sessions would break federation.
findings.why: Confirmed. Restates the universal-eduroam assumption at the attribute level as an unconditional rule. The constraint binds only adopters that actually federate via eduroam / an interfederation; stated here with no hedge ('where used'). Distinct sentence-level instance, not covered by fixing the title alone.
findings.fix: Phrase against the generic interfederation profile (\loc{identity-federation-profile}) with eduroam as the example, e.g. 'The federated-roaming technical profile (eduroam, where used) is treated as inviolate ...'.

findings.passage: a coexistence that has not been revisited in twenty-four months is reviewed against its current costs and benefits
findings.why: Confirmed. A hard-coded 24-month review cadence stated as an unconditional rule of the review mechanism. It is not a named design constant (5-dim grid / 9 layers / 10 waves), not a sourced external statistic, and not routed through any shared value or \loc. It is a programme-governance parameter baked literally into prose, liable to drift from the cadence stated in the governance chapters. The surrounding sentence is hedged ('Some institutions...') but the numeric figure itself is not.
findings.fix: Either soften to a relative phrase ('a coexistence not revisited within the programme's standing review cadence is reviewed ...') tied to the governance chapter, or, if a fixed cadence is intended, make it a single shared constant / \loc key referenced here rather than a literal in prose.

findings.passage: appearance in research-and-education-network community fora and at EDUCAUSE in recent publications
findings.why: Verified against lines 44-47. EDUCAUSE, a North-America-centric higher-education association, is named as a standing methodological filter alongside the otherwise generic 'research-and-education-network community fora'. It is not scoped as a regional example, not routed through \loc{} or a category archetype, and not hedged. The catalogue's evidentiary base therefore reads as universal but its named venue is regional, tilting it toward the US/EDUCAUSE world for every reader (a LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB or Asia-Pacific adopter has different community venues).
findings.fix: Scope EDUCAUSE explicitly as a regional example ('regional higher-education associations such as EDUCAUSE in North America') or generalise to 'regional higher-education and research-network associations', leaving EDUCAUSE as one illustrative instance rather than a universal filter.

findings.passage: national networks are mandated accordingly, a mandate documented for national operators across the region~\cite{restena,dfn,switch-nren} ... the regional research-network backbone carries the same primitives across borders~\cite{geant}
findings.why: Verified against lines 264-280. The universal claim ('A national research and education network exists to serve its country's entire research and education community... national networks are mandated accordingly') is evidenced exclusively by EU operators: RESTENA (Luxembourg), DFN (Germany), SWITCH (Switzerland) and GEANT (the European backbone). 'Across the region' silently means the EU, and the 'regional research-network backbone ... \cite{geant}' is a bare, unparameterised European interconnect presented as holding for every adopter. The citations are not labelled as a regional example and the backbone is not routed through \loc{}. A US-PUB-R1, UK-RES, LATAM-PUB or AFR-PUB reader is given EU-only precedent for a claimed-universal mandate with no regional analogue.
findings.fix: Mark the citations as a labelled regional example ('documented for European national operators, e.g.~\cite{restena,dfn,switch-nren}; comparable mandates exist in other regions') and replace the bare 'the regional research-network backbone ... \cite{geant}' with a parameterised \loc{} key (e.g. \loc{research-backbone-scale} / \loc{nren-name}) so each edition supplies its own backbone, citing GEANT only as the EU instance.

findings.passage: sector-guidance bodies already document these patterns for institutions across the size range~\cite{jisc-guidance}
findings.why: Verified against lines 282-287. The claim is universal ('sector-guidance bodies already document these patterns') but the sole evidence is Jisc, the UK sector body. Jisc is not labelled as a regional instance, not hedged, and not parameterised. For a non-UK adopter a single-jurisdiction body is presented as the proof of a generic 'sector-guidance bodies' claim.
findings.fix: Frame Jisc as one labelled regional instance ('sector-guidance bodies such as Jisc in the UK~\cite{jisc-guidance}, and their regional analogues elsewhere') so the universal claim does not rest on a single-jurisdiction body.

findings.passage: EDUCAUSE ... The principal venue for higher-education IT discussion in North America. Top 10 IT issues, governance case material ... inform several of the institutional-precedent claims
findings.why: Verified in context (lines 153-158). Although EDUCAUSE itself is described as a North-America venue, its Top 10 and governance material is presented as an unscoped generic input to the architecture's institutional-precedent claims, with no signpost to the equivalent sector body other families rely on (e.g. UCISA in the UK, regional consortia for LATAM-PUB/AFR-PUB/EU-PUB-RI). The geographic label scopes the organisation, not the precedent-base claim, biasing the precedent base toward one family.
findings.fix: Scope the precedent input as an example: 'In North-American higher education, EDUCAUSE is a principal venue ...; equivalent sector bodies (e.g.\ UCISA in the UK, regional consortia elsewhere) play the analogous role in other jurisdictions.' Optionally route the sector-venue role through a \loc{} key or category archetype.

findings.passage: REN-ISAC ... The Research and Education Networks Information Sharing and Analysis Center provides incident-response intelligence and coordination patterns referenced in
findings.why: Verified in context (lines 160-163). REN-ISAC (a US/North-America R&E ISAC) is named with NO geographic scoping at all -- unlike the adjacent EDUCAUSE entry -- and presented as the generic source of the IR intelligence and coordination patterns the architecture references. The localization registry already abstracts this role via \loc{nren-csirt} / \loc{national-gov-csirt}, so other families have a regional NREN CSIRT / sector ISAC.
findings.fix: Add a scoping clause ('in the North-American context; the analogous role elsewhere is the regional NREN CSIRT, see \loc{nren-csirt}') or present REN-ISAC as one labelled exemplar of a research-and-education ISAC.

findings.passage: GDPR ... are the principal regulatory anchors of the data dimension of the sovereignty grid. ... the principal anchor of the data-dimension scoring in the sovereignty grid.
findings.why: Verified in context (lines 114-115, 128-130). Despite the 'European regulatory framework' section heading scoping the references as European, the prose asserts that EU-only instruments (GDPR Art.32/25/35; Schrems II C-311/18) ARE 'the principal regulatory anchor' / 'the principal anchor of the data-dimension scoring' of the sovereignty grid as an architectural property, not 'for EU adopters'. The sovereignty grid is core subject (not itself a defect), but pinning its data-dimension scoring to EU-only law is unscoped; US-PRIV/US-PUB/LATAM/AFR adopters score against HIPAA/FERPA/state law, LGPD, POPIA, abstracted as \loc{data-protection-regime} / \loc{cross-border-transfer-regime}.
findings.fix: Frame the anchoring claim conditionally: 'For adopters under the EU data-protection regime these instruments anchor the data-dimension scoring; the generic data dimension is scored against \loc{data-protection-regime} / \loc{cross-border-transfer-regime}, of which GDPR and Schrems II are the EU instantiation.'

findings.passage: NIS2 Directive ... the management-body accountability for security measures (Art.~20), inform the institutional sovereignty dimension and the wave-0 governance discipline.
findings.why: Verified in context (lines 117-123). NIS2 (an EU directive) is stated to 'inform the institutional sovereignty dimension and the wave-0 governance discipline' as a generic architectural property; the informing-of-the-architecture claim is unscoped rather than 'for adopters in NIS2 scope'. Non-EU families (US, LATAM, AFR, post-Brexit UK) derive management-body accountability from a different instrument; the registry abstracts this as \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime} / \loc{essential-entity-classification-basis}.
findings.fix: Scope the claim: 'For adopters in NIS2 scope, the management-body accountability of Art.~20 informs the institutional sovereignty dimension; generically this maps to \loc{cybersecurity-baseline-regime}.' Present NIS2 as the EU instantiation of the baseline-regime role.

findings.passage: the regulatory provisions and normative controls most likely to apply to a research-intensive university
findings.why: "research-intensive university" is hard-coded as the chapter's standing addressee in the caveatbox (l.32-33), the engineering-question framing (l.44), the perimeter prose (l.86), and three table captions/intros (l.301, 442, 456). Confirmed in-file: none of these call \loc{}. The shared registry already defines institution-type = "a typical research-intensive institution" (verified in shared/localization-defaults.tex), the exact parameter for this addressee. An edition binding a non-research-intensive archetype (LATAM-PUB, AFR-PUB, a teaching-led US-PUB) cannot retarget the addressee without editing prose. The jurisdiction/size-invariant minimal-necessary-set principle requires the addressee phrase be parameterised, not baked in. Note this is the addressee, distinct from the (correctly labelled) EU worked-instantiation framing the chapter does carry.
findings.fix: Replace the standing-prose occurrences of "research-intensive university/universities" (caveatbox l.32-33, engineering-question l.44, perimeter l.86, and captions/intros at l.301, 442, 456) with \loc{institution-type}. Leave genuinely example-scoped uses as labelled examples.

findings.passage: A.5.7 Threat intelligence & Observability ingest; integration with REN-ISAC / sectoral feeds
findings.why: REN-ISAC is a specific North-American research-and-education ISAC, named without an example marker inside the ISO/IEC 27001 table. Unlike the GDPR/NIS2/AI-Act/eIDAS2 sections, this table is NOT an EU worked instantiation: the chapter itself (l.649-652) markets ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF 2.0 and COBIT 2019 as "adopted worldwide and independent of any single legal regime" and the lead spine for non-EU adopters. Naming REN-ISAC inside a jurisdiction-neutral framework therefore presents one region's R&E ISAC as the universal threat-intel feed; the registry already models this via nren-csirt / national-gov-csirt.
findings.fix: Generalise to "integration with the relevant R&E ISAC / sectoral threat-intel feeds (e.g. REN-ISAC)" or route via the NREN/CSIRT \loc keys, keeping REN-ISAC as a labelled example.

findings.passage: The phase-2 international university network is the natural locus for sharing transposition notes and harmonising the practical interpretation of the framework above.
findings.why: Confirmed in-file: the sentence asserts unconditionally ("is the natural locus") that a specific programmatic construct, "the phase-2 international university network", is the shared locus for every adopter. It is not hedged, not example-scoped, and not routed through any locality mechanism. An institution adopting the Reference standalone, or one in any archetype family not party to such a network, has no "phase-2 network"; the claim presumes a roadmap that is not universal.
findings.fix: Soften to a conditional/generic: "Where adopters cooperate (for example through an international university network), that forum is a natural locus for sharing transposition notes...", scoping it as an optional collaboration pattern rather than an assumed shared body.

findings.passage: the institution's CIO office would be expected to consolidate a complete mapping in its IT governance documentation
findings.why: "the institution's CIO office" hard-codes a specific governance-role title in standing prose. Confirmed not routed through \loc{}. Governance role labels vary by institution/family and the registry already parameterises leadership roles (executive-leadership, governing-board verified in shared/localization-defaults.tex); some adopters have no CIO office. The mild "would be expected to" hedge does not parameterise the hard-coded role title.
findings.fix: Generalise to "the institution's IT-governance function" or route via a \loc role key so editions bind their actual structure.
